newsitem.title: CHINA: China needs new proposal to enter WTO says chief.
newsitem.headline: China needs new proposal to enter WTO says chief.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) Director General Renato Ruggiero said on Monday he hoped to make clear during talks with Chinese officials that Beijing must come up with a new, credible proposal if it is to win entry.

"I really hope to give the sense that we have not to lose momentum and we are really waiting for a new and big credible proposal of China," Ruggiero told Reuters before beginning his first full day of talks in Beijing.

Diplomats from countries involved in Beijing's crucial bilateral talks on WTO entry said they had seen little change in recent months in China's position on fundamental issues holding up its application.
However, Ruggiero has said negotiations on China's entry to the world trade body were now in their final stage.

"We'll give to the Chinese authorities the awareness that we have to build on this favourable momentum of the negotiations," he said when asked what he planned to discuss in meetings with senior Chinese leaders in Beijing this week.
"So we must get from China a credible and good proposal on market access as, of course, we have to make new progress on the protocol," he said.
Ruggiero is to hold talks with Vice Premier Li Lanqing and Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi on Monday, and meets Premier Li Peng on Tuesday. He leaves on Wednesday.

China is locked in bilateral negotiations with WTO member nations on entry, with market access a particular stumbling block, diplomats said. Beijing must also agree to provisions in the WTO protocol to win entry.
Chinese and Western negotiators said last month they had made progress on Beijing's 10-year-old application for membership of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor, the WTO.
However, a wide array of barriers remain to be tackled, diplomats and analysts say.

Diplomats cited a virtual impasse on issues ranging from opening of China's agriculture markets, financial services, trading rights and distribution systems to clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry.

Some countries are demanding further cuts in China's tariff barriers. Others say it has yet to come up with even an offer on opening its securities and insurance industries, among its most tightly protected sectors.

Areas where China has yet to meet demands from Europe, Japan and the United States include trading rights -- allowing foreign firms to engage in imports and exports in China -- and national treatment on distribution.

Other China monopolies that unite developed nations in negotiations with Beijing are financial services -- prising open the banking sector -- and accounting, law firms, education and tourism and travel.
Diplomats warned that if China did not win entry soon it could find itself without a voice as the WTO makes the rules for trade into the next century.
"If they gain entry only after the rules are made then they will have to abide by rules in whose creation they have had no say," said one Western diplomat.
